articles.title: Decades of industrial pollution left Michigan’s Detroit and Kalamazoo rivers contaminated with PCBs, mercury and other chemicals; the state is now committing $89 million to clean and restore the waterways by 2040
articles.summary: For much of the 20th century, factories and paper mills along Michigan's Detroit and Kalamazoo rivers discharged waste that settled into the sediment and
articles.body: For much of the 20th century, factories and paper mills along Michigan's Detroit and Kalamazoo rivers discharged waste that settled into the sediment and lingered for decades. The legacy includes polychlorinated biphenyls, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, mercury and other pollutants that have kept both waterways on the US Environmental Protection Agency's list of Great Lakes areas of concern. In October 2026, Governor Gretchen Whitmer announced an $89 million commitment called Reclaim the Rivers to address that contamination and restore habitat, with a goal of achieving transformational change on both rivers by 2040, according to state officials and local reporting. State official screenshot and local reporting name and link to be addedA public-private push led by EGLE and DNRThe Reclaim the Rivers initiative is being led by the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, known as EGLE, and the Michigan Department of Natural Resources. The two agencies will coordinate sediment cleanup, habitat restoration, and projects that expand public access for boating, fishing and other recreation. The announcement was made on Detroit's Belle Isle, a symbolic location where the Detroit River meets Lake Erie and where restoration efforts have been visible for years.State officials describe the $89 million as seed funding that will help secure hundreds of millions of dollars in additional resources over the next 15 years. EGLE Director Phil Roos said, as per Michigan Public, the initiative is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform two of Michigan's most important waterways. The money comes from pollution settlements with companies including Monsanto and the operator of the former Morrow Dam, linking the cleanup directly to the industries that contributed to the contamination.How the money will be spentAbout $50 million of the package is earmarked for addressing polychlorinated biphenyls, or PCBs, in the Detroit River. Much of that funding will support the removal of toxic sediment from targeted areas where industrial waste accumulated over decades. Cleaning this sediment is a prerequisite for restoring fish habitat and improving water quality in sections of the river that have long carried fish consumption advisories, as per reports.Another $25 million is allocated to restoration projects in the Kalamazoo River watershed. That work includes sediment remediation, dam-related cleanup, and habitat improvements designed to support fish and wildlife.The remaining $14 million will fund restoration efforts at other waterways across the state, ensuring that communities beyond Detroit and Kalamazoo also benefit from the initiative.The Kalamazoo River's long struggle with PCBsThe Kalamazoo River has been shaped by paper manufacturing for more than a century. De-inking operations at mills in Otsego, Allegan, and Kalamazoo generated PCB-laden waste that entered the river and settled in impoundments behind dams. Over time, those contaminated sediments spread across roughly 80 miles of the river, affecting water, floodplain soils and wildlife, as per Epa.gov.Federal and state agencies have already overseen significant cleanup work, including the removal of more than 23,000 cubic yards of PCB-contaminated sediment and soil from upland floodplain areas. Dam removals and habitat restoration have followed in some sections, but complete remediation remains a long-term project. The new state funding is intended to accelerate that work and help move the river closer to delisting as an area of concern.The Detroit River and its industrial legacyThe Detroit River forms part of the international border between the United States and Canada and serves as a key connector between Lake St. Clair and Lake Erie. Heavy industry along its banks released pollutants that settled into harbors, channels and backwaters. Black Lagoon in Trenton, for example, required sediment removal in 2005 to address contamination that included PCBs, mercury, zinc, lead, and oil and grease. Recent projects have begun to reverse some of that damage. A 2026 partnership brought $10 million to tackle contaminated sediment in the Upper Trenton Harbor and other sites along the Detroit River. The Reclaim the Rivers investment builds on that momentum by providing a larger, coordinated funding stream that can support multiple sites and link cleanup to broader habitat and access improvements.What restoration looks like on the groundSediment removal is the most visible and technically complex part of the work. Proper management of dredging operations is essential to prevent the re-suspension of contaminants and the safe disposal of cleaned material. Once toxic sediment has been addressed, agencies can turn their attention to restoring natural shorelines, replanting native vegetation and building structures that support fish spawning and nesting birds. Improving public access is another key piece of the puzzle. The initiative envisions expanding boat launches, fishing piers and trails connecting communities to the rivers. These features are intended to encourage swimming, boating, and other activities that were once limited by pollution and degraded habitat. By tying cleanup to recreation, the state hopes to make the rivers central to local identity and economic development.A 15-year horizon with 2040 as a targetEGLE and DNR expect the Reclaim the Rivers work to unfold over about 15 years, with 2040 set as the target for lasting, transformational change on both rivers. That timeline reflects the scale of the contamination and the need to coordinate with federal programs, local governments and private partners. Progress will be measured not only by the volume of sediment removed but also by improvements in water quality, fish populations and public use. Both the Detroit and Kalamazoo rivers are designated EPA areas of concern under the Great Lakes Restoration framework. Delisting requires that all beneficial use impairments, such as restrictions on fishing or swimming, be resolved. The $89 million commitment is designed to move both waterways closer to that goal by addressing the most stubborn sources of pollution and creating conditions for ecosystems to recover.Why it matters for communities and the Great LakesFor people living along the Detroit River and Kalamazoo River, the initiative is a chance to restore waterways that have been inaccessible or underused for generations. Improved sediment quality and habitat health can increase fish populations, helping to reduce consumption advisories and resume traditional fishing practices. Enhanced access can also attract visitors and support local businesses reliant on river-based recreation. At a larger scale, the health of these rivers affects the entire Great Lakes system, with the Detroit River serving as a major water flow corridor and migratory species route, and the Kalamazoo River being a crucial part of Lake Michigan’s ecosystem. Investing in their restoration helps protect regional biodiversity and prevents the legacy of industrial pollution from shaping the future of these iconic waterways.

articles.title: Vessev built an electric ferry that almost flies
articles.summary: Vessev hopes its electric hydrofoil ferry will change the way people and cities think about boats.
articles.body:
“When will we start flying?” I asked Vessev co-founder and CEO Eric Laakmann, as we pulled away from the Brooklyn marina in the startup’s VS-9 electric ferry. “We already are.”

I’ll admit I was a bit disappointed. I thought the moment when it transitioned from sailing like a regular boat to almost-flying as a surface-skimming hydrofoil would be more … momentous.

I’ve been on my share of boats, including large ferries, small sailboats, and plenty of others in between, but never been on a hydrofoil and I was curious what flying along the water might feel like during the brief ride from the Brooklyn Marina out toward Governors Island on the East River in New York.

It didn’t feel like flying, but it was a bit like a riding in a sports car.

Traditional boats of this size — about 30 feet — start to bounce and slap the water as they gain speed. But on a hydrofoil, that’s when the foils start to do their work.

On the surface, the VS-9 looks like plenty of other catamarans. But under the hull are two wing-like structures that lift the boat as they slice through the water. Computer-controlled underwater flaps keep the ride smooth and stable. In the VS-9, most of the lifting is done by the front foil, with about 20% handled by the rear.

The rear foil also hosts the electric motor, which Vessev makes in-house. Why not outsource it? Laakmann said that it’s important to keep costs in line — eventually, you’ll have to bring production in house, so why not do it earlier in development? The only thing Vessev doesn’t build are the batteries. “Those have been commoditized,” Laakmann said.

By lifting the hull clear of the water, hydrofoils can operate more efficiently than other boats. That’s especially important for electric boats, where every kilowatt-hour counts.

Shipbuilders have been experimenting with hydrofoils for well over a century. The design offers several advantages, including lower drag and a smoother ride. The subtle transition I experienced on the VS-9, from sailing to almost-flying, underlined just how smooth a hydrofoil can be.

Despite hydrofoils’ advantages, they’re not a panacea. The design works best in waters the boat can clear when sailing on its foils. For the VS-9, that’s about two and a half feet, or 0.75 meters. If the waves go higher than that, they start hitting the hull, ruining the smooth ride and sapping some efficiency. While they’re not ideal for the open ocean, hydrofoils make sense for other waterways, including lakes, rivers, and bays.

Vessev, which raised a $19 million Series A in August, is targeting transit operations to start. Laakmann thinks the combination of electric propulsion and hydrofoils can bring down the cost of operating smaller vessels and make them comfortable enough that they could augment urban mass transit systems.

Somewhere like New York City could use them to zip people to Brooklyn or Queens without needing to build much new infrastructure.

Hotels and tour operators are also an early target market, and public demonstrations like the one I attended have attracted wealthy individuals looking for another toy, Laakmann said.

For now, the VS-9 I rode is one of a kind, but Laakmann said Vessev plans to build more. Eventually, the company might shift to producing electric hydrofoil kits, allowing other boatbuilders to design their own vessels around the technology, Laakmann said.

articles.title: Georgia has begun a 10-year restoration of 132 acres at Towaliga Preserve, using a data-centre partnership to rebuild forest habitat on one of Henry County's largest undeveloped properties
articles.summary: A 132-acre section of one of Henry County, Georgia’s largest remaining undeveloped properties is set for a 10-year forest restoration project, with a
articles.body: A 132-acre section of one of Henry County, Georgia’s largest remaining undeveloped properties is set for a 10-year forest restoration project, with a data-centre company funding the effort as part of a broader environmental partnership. The Southern Conservation Trust (SCT) is leading the restoration at Towaliga Preserve, a 403-acre protected property in Hampton, with support from QTS Data Centres.The initiative, announced by SCT and reported by The Citizen, will focus on restoring 77 acres of degraded, early-successional forest and improving another 52 acres of mature forest through targeted removal of invasive plants. QTS's support comes through a 10-year commitment connected to Phase 2 of its Fayetteville data-centre campus and its Tree Replacement Program.From farmland to protected forestTowaliga Preserve, formerly known as Henderson Farms, covers about 403 acres and is owned and protected by the Southern Conservation Trust. The property includes oak-hickory-pine forests, mesic and bottomland hardwood forests, wetlands and streams, as well as approximately 1.5 miles of the upper Towaliga River. The landscape has not always been forested. Parts of the property were historically used for cattle grazing and forestry. About 72 acres of forest were harvested around 2015, before SCT acquired the property, according to the conservation trust.Since then, the cleared areas have naturally regenerated. But the resulting young forest is dominated not only by native species such as sweetgum and tulip poplar, but also by invasive non-native plants including privet, Chinaberry and Oriental bittersweet. The new restoration effort is intended to change that balance. Rather than simply adding trees to the property, the project will involve managing an existing forest ecosystem and encouraging a more diverse and healthier landscape.What will happen over the next decade?The restoration will begin with site preparation, including removing several thousand feet of old barbed-wire fencing. Starting in fall 2026, professional forestry contractors are scheduled to carry out staged thinning and mulching across about 77 acres. Targeted treatment of invasive vegetation will follow in 2027, with native tree planting planned for winter 2027-28. Another approximately 52 acres of mature forest will receive targeted invasive-species management beginning in fall 2026.SCT says the work will involve ongoing monitoring rather than a one-time planting campaign. The organisation will oversee contractors, direct restoration activities, and adjust management based on how the forest responds. The conservation trust also plans to continue caring for the property after the 10-year implementation period ends.“We’re not planting trees and walking away,” SCT President and CEO Chris Doane said in the announcement, emphasising that the organisation's stewardship of Towaliga Preserve will continue beyond the formal project period.Data centre company expands conservation partnershipThe restoration is being funded through a partnership between SCT and QTS Data Centres, a company developing data-centre infrastructure in the region. QTS's relationship with SCT began in 2023 and has already supported reforestation, land stewardship, environmental education and volunteer activities.The new project follows an earlier restoration effort at Towaliga Preserve. During Phase 1, SCT and QTS supported the planting of 12,140 native trees representing 21 species across a 23-acre former agricultural field. The original target was at least 7,000 trees, meaning the project exceeded its initial planting goal. That earlier project also became a research opportunity.SCT is working with the University of Georgia to study tree survival and growth across four research plots containing 576 trees from 21 species. Researchers are examining how different species and planting methods perform under the site's conditions. The results are intended to help inform the larger restoration now getting underway.Why the forest mattersThe restoration comes as development continues to transform parts of Henry County. The Towaliga Preserve provides a connected landscape of forests, wetlands and waterways at a time when residential and other development is changing surrounding areas. SCT says the project is intended to improve wildlife habitat and native plant diversity while supporting the health of the Towaliga River watershed.Forest restoration can also have effects beyond the trees themselves. SCT says the work is expected to help reduce erosion and improve water infiltration, while healthier forest habitat can support a wider variety of native plants and wildlife. The preserved landscape also creates opportunities for environmental education, ecological research, wildlife observation and outdoor recreation. The approximately 1.5 miles of the upper Towaliga River running through the preserve is another reason the condition of the surrounding land matters.A longer-term conservation experimentThe project is also being framed as an opportunity to learn what restoration methods work best in the region. The research from the first QTS-supported planting effort is expected to help SCT select species and approaches for the much larger Phase 2 project. That means the 10-year effort will involve both restoration and continued observation of how the forest develops.For QTS, the partnership provides a way to connect its regional development with conservation work. The company says its support is intended to strengthen forest ecosystems, biodiversity and long-term environmental benefits in communities where it operates. The project does not mean all 403 acres of Towaliga Preserve are being replanted. The 132-acre figure refers to the specific area targeted under the new restoration initiative, while the broader preserve remains a protected 403-acre property.As the first contractors begin work in fall 2026, the restoration will therefore unfold gradually rather than producing an immediate new forest. The first changes will involve removing fencing, thinning selected areas and controlling invasive vegetation. Native trees are scheduled to be planted later, while researchers and conservationists monitor how the landscape responds.Over the next decade, the aim is to turn portions of a young, heavily disturbed forest into a more diverse and resilient habitat, while keeping the larger Towaliga Preserve protected for the future.

articles.title: NASA report shows how Nepal rains triggered Bihar floods: Minister
articles.summary: NASA satellite report says heavy Sept 24-27 rains in Nepal’s Gandak catchment raised river levels, causing Bihar floods; relief and barrage discharges monitored.
articles.body: Patna: Citing a NASA Earth Observatory report based on satellite imagery, deputy CM and water resources department (WRD) minister Vijay Kumar Choudhary on Saturday said heavy rainfall in the Gandak’s catchment areas in Nepal between Sept 24 and 27 led to a sharp rise in the river’s water level, contributing to flooding in its downstream districts in Bihar.“According to the NASA report, there was unprecedented heavy rain in the hilly areas of Lumbini and the Gandak catchment in Nepal from Sept 24 to 27. It led to landslides and a record rise in the level of the Gandak, known as Narayani in Nepal, both there and in the Bihar portion of the river,” Choudhary said.He said the floodwaters spread downstream in Bihar, overtopping embankments at several places and breaching them at a few locations. The impact was particularly visible in West Champaran, Gopalganj, Muzaffarpur and Saran, he added.Choudhary said the report, titled ‘Rains Swamp the Gandak River’, was published by NASA Earth Observatory on Oct 2 and he compared satellite images from Sept 20 and 29 to show the extent of flooding along the river.According to Choudhary, the Gandak at Devghat in Nepal reached 11.94 metres on Sept 27, its highest level since the gauge station was established in the 1960s.He also said the report noted that the river crossed the highest flood level (HFL) at Bagaha in West Champaran, Dumariaghat in Gopalganj, Rewaghat in Saran and Lalganj in Vaishali.Choudhary said the state govt was maintaining a close watch on the flood situation and embankments and was focusing on rescue and relief operations in affected districts.Meanwhile, water discharge through the Valmikinagar barrage on the Gandak, Birpur barrage on the Kosi and Indrapuri barrage on the Sone had fallen to 73,400 cusecs, 80,745 cusecs and 39,307 cusecs, respectively. The Ganga was flowing above the danger level at four places, while the Kosi was above it at two places and the Bagmati and Burhi Gandak at one place each.IAF choppers drop 5,600 relief packetsTwo IAF helicopters deployed for relief operations have so far airdropped more than 5,600 packets of dry ration, weighing around 28 tonnes, in inaccessible and difficult-to-reach areas of flood-hit Saran, the disaster management department (DMD) said on Saturday.The DMD said it had approached the Union home and defence ministries for IAF helicopters following a directive from CM Samrat Choudhary. articles.title: A 10.22-kg rock used as a Michigan barn doorstop for decades was identified as a new iron meteorite
articles.summary: A meteorite that spent decades as a barn doorstop in Michigan has been identified as a new IIIAB iron meteorite.
articles.body: A meteorite that spent decades as a barn doorstop in Michigan has been identified as a new IIIAB iron meteorite. The 10.22-kilogram rock reportedly fell on a farm near Edmore in 1939. After a different meteorite fell near Hamburg, Michigan, in 2018, the farm's later owners, who had been told the rock's story, recognized its value to science and brought it to Central Michigan University for identification.According to the research presented at the 50th Lunar and Planetary Science Conference in 2019, a slice was later studied at the Smithsonian Institution, where scientists analysed its composition and internal structure. The meteorite, which had been found near Edmore in 1939 and used as a doorstop for decades, was later named Edmore, Michigan, as its officially approved meteorite name.The rock found in 1939 was later identified as a meteoriteThe Edmore meteorite was found on a farm near the town of Edmore in Michigan in 1939. The owner reportedly recovered it and later used the stone as a doorstop for a barn. The farm’s subsequent owners had been told the story of the unusual rock and later brought it to Central Michigan University for identification.After the Hamburg, Michigan, fall in early 2018, the subsequent owners recognised that the old stone could have scientific value. They took it to Central Michigan University in Mt. Pleasant for identification. The specimen is triangular and measures 17 x 20 x 23 cm. It weighs 10.22 kg and has large surface indentations. Portions of its surface have a light brown fusion crust.Scientists examined the meteorite’s internal structureA slice of the meteorite was sent to the Smithsonian Institution for identification and classification. Scientists used a Nova NanoSEM 600 scanning electron microscope under low vacuum and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy to identify nickel in the sample. They then prepared the slice with 10% Nital and alcohol to expose its Widmanstätten pattern.The meteorite was described as a medium octahedrite. The examined slice contained kamacite, taenite, and schreibersite. Kamacite lamellae within the Widmanstätten structure were about 0.8 mm wide. The taenite between the kamacite lamellae showed pronounced zoning. Schreibersite grains reached up to 4 mm in width and showed extensive fracturing.Results:Edmore became an officially recognised meteoriteThe researchers noted that Edmore is a new IIIAB iron meteorite based on the information and analyses presented in the study. The paper states that the iridium data were particularly important in reaching this conclusion. Edmore, Michigan, is the approved name for the meteorite.Its identification also draws attention to meteorites that may remain in personal collections without their owners knowing their scientific importance. The researchers noted that the Edmore case, like the 2018 Hamburg fall, shows why greater public visibility of meteorites can help bring new specimens forward for study.

articles.title: Noah's Ark researchers ‘inching towards’ confirmation after drilling challenges natural-rock theory
articles.summary: Noah's Ark Scans founder Andrew Jones says core drilling near Mount Ararat found no bedrock but revealed black soil with potentially rich organic matter.
articles.body: A team investigating a boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey says new evidence is strengthening its case that the site could hold the remains of Noah's Ark. "In archaeology, you deal with probabilities, and we're inching towards where we believe we will have confirmation this winter after our soil analysis is done with Sivas University, who's our partner in this," Noah's Ark Scans founder Andrew Jones told "Saturday in America." The focus of the investigation is the Durupınar formation, an approximately 538-foot-long geological structure near Mount Ararat. Its shape and proximity to the region identified in the biblical account have fascinated Ark hunters for decades. The boat-shaped formation was first discovered in 1959 and has long-drawn speculation over a possible connection to Noah's Ark. SITE WHERE JESUS WAS CRUCIFIED AND BURIED REVEALS NEW EVIDENCE THAT BACKS BIBLICAL ACCOUNT Critics have maintained that the formation is naturally occurring, but Jones said recent drilling, soil sampling and ground-penetrating radar have given his team new reasons to challenge that conclusion. "They've criticized in the past, saying all those scans you can interpret different ways, 'This is a solid mass of rock, a syncline or a block of bedrock,'" Jones said. "Well, we've core drilled… over 12 locations. We did not find bedrock at all." AUTHOR DINESH D'SOUZA CHALLENGES BIBLE SKEPTICS WITH 'STARTLING' ARCHAEOLOGICAL DISCOVERIES Jones said the drilling uncovered rich black soil, which researchers plan to test for organic content this winter at Ankara University. "Noah's Ark was a giant wooden boat, according to the Bible," he said. "As wood decays, you're gonna find elevated organic matter. This year, as we drilled into the formation, we did not find a solid rock layer, like the critics said. But we did find large deposits of highly rich black soil that has hopefully high organics." The researchers hope the analysis will help determine whether there are signs of human activity or materials consistent with decayed wood beneath the formation. Researchers investigating a boat-shaped formation in Turkey believe they are close to confirming it as Noah's Ark based on new evidence from soil analysis with Sivas University.

The Durupınar formation near Mount Ararat has long been speculated to be the remains of Noah's Ark, with recent drilling and ground-penetrating radar challenging critics who argue it is a natural rock formation.

Soil analysis from the site has revealed chemical differences consistent with decayed organic material, with researchers planning to test the rich black soil for organic content at Ankara University this winter.

A team investigating a boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey says new evidence is strengthening its case that the site could hold the remains of Noah's Ark.

"In archaeology, you deal with probabilities, and we're inching towards where we believe we will have confirmation this winter after our soil analysis is done with Sivas University, who's our partner in this," Noah's Ark Scans founder Andrew Jones told "Saturday in America."

The focus of the investigation is the Durupınar formation, an approximately 538-foot-long geological structure near Mount Ararat. Its shape and proximity to the region identified in the biblical account have fascinated Ark hunters for decades.

The boat-shaped formation was first discovered in 1959 and has long-drawn speculation over a possible connection to Noah's Ark.

Critics have maintained that the formation is naturally occurring, but Jones said recent drilling, soil sampling and ground-penetrating radar have given his team new reasons to challenge that conclusion.

"They've criticized in the past, saying all those scans you can interpret different ways, 'This is a solid mass of rock, a syncline or a block of bedrock,'" Jones said. "Well, we've core drilled… over 12 locations. We did not find bedrock at all."

Jones said the drilling uncovered rich black soil, which researchers plan to test for organic content this winter at Ankara University .

"Noah's Ark was a giant wooden boat, according to the Bible," he said.

"As wood decays, you're gonna find elevated organic matter. This year, as we drilled into the formation, we did not find a solid rock layer, like the critics said. But we did find large deposits of highly rich black soil that has hopefully high organics."

The researchers hope the analysis will help determine whether there are signs of human activity or materials consistent with decayed wood beneath the formation.

articles.title: Scientists resurrected 160-million-year-old proteins from extinct mammals; some were stronger against drug-resistant bacteria than modern human versions, raising new hopes for antibiotic research
articles.summary: There is an unexpected place scientists are looking for clues to the next generation of infection-fighting drugs: deep in the evolutionary past.
articles.body: There is an unexpected place scientists are looking for clues to the next generation of infection-fighting drugs: deep in the evolutionary past. At the University of Oregon, researchers reconstructed proteins that existed as far back as 160 million years ago and found that some of their antimicrobial fragments could outperform corresponding versions found in humans when tested against drug-resistant bacteria, states a release shared by Science Daily. The research, published in PLOS Biology on August 25, offers a glimpse into how nature refined its own defence mechanisms over millions of years and how those evolutionary experiments could potentially inform future treatments for infections that no longer respond well to conventional antibiotics.Searching the mammalian pastThe study focused on lactoferrin, an immune protein found in almost every body fluid except blood, including breast milk, tears, saliva and intestinal mucus. One of its best-known functions is to bind iron, effectively depriving bacteria of a resource they need to grow. But lactoferrin has another weapon. Buried within the protein is a short antimicrobial peptide capable of attacking bacterial membranes and creating holes that can damage or destroy microbial cells.Researchers wanted to understand when this ability emerged and how it changed as mammals evolved. Their investigation took them back to the earliest ancestors of placental mammals, a group that eventually gave rise to humans and most mammals alive today.Reconstructing extinct biologyUsing genetic sequences from living animals, including humans and cows, the team mapped lactoferrin's evolutionary relationships and used ancestral sequence reconstruction to predict what versions of the protein's genes may have looked like millions of years ago. The predicted genes were then synthesized and used to produce the reconstructed proteins in the laboratory. Researchers tested the resulting antimicrobial peptides against several bacteria associated with human disease, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli and Streptococcus.The oldest reconstructed peptides could damage bacterial membranes, but the bacteria were often able to repair themselves and survive. As researchers moved forward through evolutionary time, however, the peptides became progressively more potent. Some versions originating from relatively recent mammalian ancestors were even more effective against certain drug-resistant bacteria than the corresponding modern human peptides, the release said.The power of one small mutationOne of the study's most intriguing findings was how little genetic change was sometimes required to produce a major difference in antimicrobial activity. Researchers found that a single mutation in the amino-acid sequence could substantially enhance the peptide's ability to attack bacteria. The discovery highlights how small evolutionary changes can dramatically reshape biological functions over time.For scientists, that makes evolution more than a historical record. It becomes a vast catalogue of natural experiments, preserving evidence of which molecular changes worked and which did not, adds the online release.A long road to new treatmentsThe findings do not mean that ancient peptides are ready to replace antibiotics. The researchers note that antimicrobial peptides can be less structurally stable than conventional drugs and may be broken down quickly inside the human body. Their immediate value may instead lie in providing blueprints for new molecules. Looking at the evolution of antimicrobial defenses, the researchers were able to pinpoint structural modifications that have made these peptides more potent and potentially develop treatments that work alongside existing antibiotics.The method could also help scientists predict how bacteria might develop resistance to new antimicrobial agents. Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of these ancient biological weapons could eventually help researchers develop therapies that are more difficult for pathogens to escape. In the escalating war against drug-resistant infections, the past may hold surprising value, not as an ancient medicine waiting to be rediscovered, but as an evolutionary blueprint for designing new ones.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: Queen's University Belfast students head to US for Nasa competition
articles.summary: The students will head to Florida to compete against university teams from Australia, India and the US.
articles.body:
Could a robot designed by young engineering students from Northern Ireland end up on the Moon?

A team, from Queen's University Belfast (QUB), are heading to Florida later this month to take part in a Nasa 'lunabotics' competition.

Lunabotics is a university-level competition for teams to use the Nasa systems engineering process to design, build, and operate a lunar robot.

The students created a lab-built robot that they will bring to the competition to find out how it would deal with future moon missions.

The robots will be expected to dig up lunar material, drive over obstacles and use the material to form a wall.

Jack Fitzpatrick, who's studying for a PhD in mechanical engineering, said "it's a great feeling" to have been invited and they're looking forward to the opportunity to take part.

The team of 10 QUB students made it to the competition following their win at the competition earlier this year.

They'll be competing at the University of Central Florida against university teams from Australia, India and the US.

Jamie Smith is a third-year electrical and electronic engineering student.

He explained that the team was divided into three groups for software, electronics and mechanical.

Jamie was the software team lead for this project. He said their main task was to control the rover then provide the autonomous capabilities towards it.

And, they had to build rover simulations to test their software before they actually got one.

Jack, however, is part of the mechanical side.

"We analyse that something is physically strong enough, it's well built enough to survive this environment, it's going to have the traction to drive in this environment," he explained.

Jamie explained they designed the 52 kg aluminium frame robot rover and took it compete at a competition in Milton Keynes.

"We got on very well. We ended up winning the competition and had great fun," he said.

Then a few weeks later, they were invited to compete at Nasa's international Lunabotics competition.

Jack said that being asked to go was a "great feeling" and "a real opportunity to demonstrate everything that you've learned".

"It's just a great opportunity to represent Northern Ireland, the UK and really Europe abroad as we are the only European team that will be there," Jack explained.

Both of the students said their success was a reflection of both themselves and also the university and the School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering.

Jamie explained that the main objective of the rover is that should be able to drive itself around a lunar-simulated room.

"That means it should start at a point, figure out where it is within this room, travel to an excavation point, so in that point, it will pick up then some sand which is meant to be lunar-simulant.

"It'll pick up the sand and then deposit it at another location, and it's meant to do this all by itself."

Jack explained that the purpose of this is to simulate how real rovers carry out these kind of tasks on the moon.

"It's being able to autonomously operate on the moon and build environments for humans to later habitat. And that's the real drive behind why this competition exists," he explained.

So are they feeling confident they can bring home another win?

Jack explained that there have been several precursor competitions in different countries and this competition takes the top tier of those competitions and brings them together "to really showcase the talent" that there is internationally.

"We are the winning team from the United Kingdom competition and we will be representing the UK and, by extension, Europe at this competition."

"We may not win the competition this year but we're building a base upon which we can improve year on year and maybe come back in a few years and really come through with a winning design," he said.

Caolán Boyle, Head of Robotics at QPL, said the team is "exceptionally proud and excited".

He said "hundreds of hours have gone into making the rover mission ready for the event".

articles.title: Trust warns of 'tangible' climate threat to North Yorkshire heritage sites
articles.summary: A National Trust manager says recent summers have "brought home" the impact of climate change.
articles.body:
Protecting all heritage sites from the impact of climate change "just may not be possible," according to a National Trust manager.

Justin Scully, manager of Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal, said extreme heat, heavy rainfall and wildfire risk were already affecting gardens, moorland and historic structures.

He said heavy rain could overwhelm drainage systems and penetrate walls, causing damp and erosion, while repeated cycles of wetting, drying, freezing and thawing could harm stonework.

Flooding could also undermine foundations, while hotter, dry conditions could increase the risk of subsidence and wildfires.

Scully said the organisation may have to accept it cannot save everything as it is today.

"These last two summers have really brought this home to ourselves and to our visitors," he said.

"Climate change isn't a thing that's happening out there to other people, it's actually impacting ourselves and the places we love. The threat is tangible."

The National Trust is planning for more extreme weather by looking at what could happen to the properties and landscapes it manages over the next 40 years.

"We've got to think about what could be the worst possible outcome and then work backwards from that," Scully said.

At Fountains Abbey, this could include increasing drainage capacity and gutters to cope with heavier rainfall.

It could also result in changing the appearance of the gardens.

Scully said the trust needed to be "more open to how we would adapt," with gardens potentially becoming "less manicured".

"People expect things to look perfect and crisp," he said.

The trust looks after properties including Beningbrough Hall, Nunnington Hall and Treasurer's House in York, as well as miles of coastline from Loftus to Filey.

It said coastal sites were among those facing the greatest climate pressures, including erosion and rising sea levels.

A National Trust spokesperson said: "Climate change is affecting many of the places we care for, and our conservation work has to evolve with it."

Conservation decisions would consider the significance of a place, the benefit it brings to people and whether an approach is sustainable long term, they added.

The National Trust is a charity and receives no guaranteed government money, although it can apply for project grants from public bodies and lottery funds.

Scully said some adaptation processes could be "very expensive".

The trust did not give a figure for those costs, but said it would continue to invest significantly in conservation.

It also called for climate resilience to become a national priority, led by a Cabinet-level minister coordinating preparedness across government and supporting long-term investment.

"There are small things that we can do as communities [such as reducing carbon footprints] that will make a big difference over the longer term."
