articles.title: US biologists searching the Mojave Desert found six previously unknown Mojave poppy bee population groups; the new evidence helped determine the tiny specialist bee does not need endangered-species listing
articles.summary: US biologists searching the Mojave Desert have discovered six previously unknown population groups of the Mojave poppy bee, giving scientists a broader
articles.body: US biologists searching the Mojave Desert have discovered six previously unknown population groups of the Mojave poppy bee, giving scientists a broader picture of the tiny insect's distribution and helping the US Fish and Wildlife Service conclude that the species does not currently require protection under the Endangered Species Act, the agency said in an October 2, 2026 report.The discovery followed surveys conducted in 2023 and 2024 by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the US Department of Agriculture's Agricultural Research Service and other partners. The newly gathered evidence, combined with existing scientific and commercial information, helped officials assess threats to the bee and determine that it does not meet the federal definitions of threatened or endangered.A bee built around a few desert flowersThe Mojave poppy bee (Perdita meconis) is a small, solitary, ground-nesting bee found in the eastern Mojave Desert. Unlike generalist pollinators that can feed on many types of flowers, the species is a specialist associated with a small group of poppy plants.The US Fish and Wildlife Service said individual bees live for only days to a few weeks, while their survival is closely tied to the availability and flowering of their host plants. These include the Las Vegas bear poppy and several species of prickly poppy.USDA research describes the bee as a rare species restricted to the eastern Mojave Desert. Its host plants often occur in specialised gypsum-rich soils, which are scattered across the region. The bee is also remarkably small. USDA researchers said males average only 5 to 7 millimetres in length. Its tiny size is one reason the species can be difficult to locate during field surveys.Biologists went looking where records were oldScientists had reason to be concerned about the bee before the latest survey. Historic records showed the species across parts of California, Nevada, Arizona and Utah, but researchers had not recently surveyed some of those locations. The US Fish and Wildlife Service said its survey strategy therefore prioritised historic locations where the bee or its host plants had not been checked for many years.“We prioritised historic locations where surveys had not been done for many years,” Corey Kallstrom, a wildlife biologist with the US Fish and Wildlife Service's Southern Nevada Fish and Wildlife Office, said. He said the approach was designed to address places where the bee and its host plants may have been overlooked. U.S. Fish and Wildlife ServiceThe effort produced a significant result. Between 2023 and 2024, survey teams led by USDA's Pollinating Insects Research Unit identified six previously unknown population groups within the bee's historical range. The findings expanded scientists' understanding of where the insect survives and provided additional evidence about the resilience of its populations. UOne population disappeared, but six were foundThe findings were not uniformly positive. The Fish and Wildlife Service said researchers also documented the loss of one population group in Utah. Earlier USDA research had similarly found that the bee remained present at many historic locations but appeared to have disappeared from southwestern Utah.Research at Utah State University had already shown how difficult the species can be to detect. A 2023 master's thesis examining the bee and the Las Vegas bear poppy found small numbers of Mojave poppy bees at three sites in 2020, but none were detected at those sites the following year despite systematic sampling through the flowering season. Surveys in 2022 found single individuals at two of those locations. The same research documented substantial fluctuations in the Las Vegas bear poppy's populations, highlighting how conditions can change from one year to another in the desert.The bee can wait out bad conditionsOne unusual feature of the Mojave poppy bee may help explain its ability to survive the desert's boom-and-bust conditions.USDA researchers found evidence that the insect can remain underground in an immature state for at least three years, apparently allowing it to wait for more favourable conditions and the return of suitable host plants. The phenomenon is known as diapause. That adaptation is important because the poppy plants themselves can be short-lived and their populations fluctuate with environmental conditions.The bee's dependence on these plants, however, also creates a vulnerability. Scientists have identified threats including urban development, mining, habitat fragmentation, trampling and changing precipitation patterns that can affect the plants on which the bee depends.Scientists also decoded its genomeThe recent population discovery follows another major research effort involving the species. In 2024, USDA's Agricultural Research Service and university partners announced the development of a near chromosome-level reference genome for the Mojave poppy bee. Researchers said the genetic map could help scientists investigate the bee's ability to cope with drought, its specialised relationship with host plants and possible genetic signs of population decline. The genome was produced from a single male specimen collected in the field. Researchers said obtaining high-quality DNA was notable because the specimen had not been preserved under ideal conditions.Why it will not be listed as endangeredThe latest surveys were conducted partly because the Fish and Wildlife Service was evaluating whether the bee warranted protection under the Endangered Species Act. An agency peer-review plan published earlier in 2026 said the species-status assessment was intended to determine whether the Mojave poppy bee warranted listing as threatened or endangered. After considering the new population information and other available scientific and commercial data, the agency concluded that the species does not currently meet the definition of threatened or endangered and therefore does not need to be federally listed.That decision does not mean the Mojave poppy bee is considered risk-free. The Fish and Wildlife Service continues to classify conservation work for unlisted species at risk as an important part of its approach, noting that collecting information and taking proactive conservation measures can help prevent species from reaching the point where federal protection becomes necessary.

articles.title: Meet Wileidy Feliciano-Rivera, the Puerto Rico seventh-grader who turned discarded school-cafeteria plantain peels into biodegradable farm mulch that cut weed growth by up to 53% in tests
articles.summary: A Puerto Rico seventh-grader has found an unusual use for something that would normally be thrown away after lunch: plantain peels.
articles.body: A Puerto Rico seventh-grader has found an unusual use for something that would normally be thrown away after lunch: plantain peels. Wileidy Feliciano-Rivera collected discarded peels from her school cafeteria and turned them into a biodegradable mulch designed to control weeds in agricultural soil. In four-week tests, her two plantain-based mulch versions reduced weed growth by 47% and 53% compared with uncovered soil, while also helping retain moisture and lower soil temperatures. Her project has now earned her a place among the 30 finalists in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge, according to the Society for Science, the competition organiser.From cafeteria waste to an agricultural materialWileidy, a seventh-grade student at Escuela Intermedia Rafael Irizarry Rivera in Peñuelas, Puerto Rico, began the project by looking at two problems connected to agriculture: plastic waste and the disposal of organic material.Plastic mulch is used by farmers to cover soil, suppress weeds and help retain moisture. But after use, plastic mulch can become agricultural waste. Wileidy explored whether a biodegradable material could perform some of the same functions without relying on conventional plastic. Her attention turned to plantain peels being discarded at her school. Instead of treating them as waste, she investigated whether they could serve as the raw material for a bioplastic mulch. The resulting project was called EcoMusa. Its name reflects the use of Musa paradisiaca, the scientific name used in the project for the plantain source material.How Wileidy made EcoMusaThe young researcher processed the discarded plantain peels and used them to produce sheets of bioplastic. According to Society for Science, she first chopped the peels into smaller pieces before blending them with water, acetic acid, glycerin and cornstarch. The mixture was then heated and poured into trays, where it was allowed to dry and form sheets.Wileidy produced two versions of the material, known as EcoMusa 1 and EcoMusa 2. She then tested whether they could work as mulch by placing them over soil and comparing their performance with uncovered soil and commercial black plastic mulch.The experiment was designed to look at more than just whether weeds appeared. Wileidy also monitored soil moisture, soil temperature and how the plant-based material degraded during the test period.Weed growth dropped by up to 53%The experiment ran for four weeks, during which Wileidy tracked weed density in the different test areas. EcoMusa 1 reduced weed growth by 47%, while EcoMusa 2 produced a 53% reduction compared with uncovered soil. The Society for Science reported that the two versions performed comparably to the commercial black plastic mulch used in the experiment. The mulch also affected conditions beneath the soil covering. The plantain-based materials kept soil temperatures between one and three degrees Celsius lower than uncovered soil and helped retain moisture.Those results suggest that the material could perform some of the functions expected from agricultural mulch. However, the experiment was limited to four weeks, so the findings do not establish how the material would perform over a full growing season or across different crops and farming conditions.A project linking food and plastic wasteEcoMusa brings together two types of waste that are often treated separately. The plantain peels used in Wileidy's experiment were food waste from her school cafeteria. Turning them into a bioplastic mulch gave that discarded material another potential use.At the same time, the project explores an alternative to conventional plastic mulch. Because EcoMusa is biodegradable, its intended purpose is not simply to replace one form of plastic with another, but to create a material that can break down after use. The project therefore goes beyond the idea of simply making a new material. It examines whether a readily available waste product can be converted into something useful for agriculture.A place among 2026's young science finalistsWileidy's research has now taken her beyond her school laboratory. Her EcoMusa project was selected among the 30 finalists for the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. The competition, run by the Society for Science, recognises middle-school students conducting research in science, technology, engineering and mathematics. The finalists are scheduled to participate in Finals Week in Washington, DC, from October 23 to 28, with more than $100,000 in prizes available.For Wileidy, the project began with a simple observation about material being discarded at school. She turned those peels into a research question and then tested whether the resulting material could do a useful job in agriculture.What the experiment showsEcoMusa is not yet evidence that plantain-peel mulch can replace commercial agricultural plastic on a large scale. More research would be needed to determine its durability, degradation rate, performance across different environments and suitability for different crops. But Wileidy's four-week experiment produced measurable results. Her two mulch versions reduced weed growth by up to 53%, while also helping retain soil moisture and moderate soil temperature.The project demonstrates how an everyday waste product can become the starting point for a scientific experiment. What began as discarded plantain peels from a Puerto Rico school cafeteria has become a biodegradable agricultural material that Wileidy is now testing as a possible way to manage weeds while addressing waste.

articles.title: Machine learning: The conscience of the creator
articles.summary: “Of all the animals, perhaps, man is the only one who can think and perceive a phenomenon beyond the range of his senses…” So begins a lecture note from
articles.body: “Of all the animals, perhaps, man is the only one who can think and perceive a phenomenon beyond the range of his senses…” So begins a lecture note from 1972 by Satish Dhawan, widely regarded as the architect of the Indian space programme. Dhawan was speaking about remote sensing. But this quote, which has stayed with me since the first time I read it, serves us well in dealing with what we are going to deal with today.What interests me about it is the idea that we can reason about things we cannot directly perceive. We infer the existence of distant planets, invisible forces and phenomena that our senses cannot detect. But what happens when the thing we’re trying to understand isn’t out there, somewhere in the universe, but something we have created ourselves? Something that speaks our language, appears to reason like us, and can even make us wonder whether it has an inner life?Helping a machine learn how to be good appears like a worthwhile project. Until you are forced to pause by an inconvenient question: good according to whom?And that’s the sort of problem Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah appears to have found himself confronting. Anthropic makes Claude, a family of AI models that the company says it wants to behave not merely intelligently, but morally. To figure out what that might mean, Olah turned to an unlikely source of technical expertise: religious and philosophical thinkers.The conversations, described in a recent New York Times report by Elizabeth Dias, ranged from virtue and moral formation to a question that is considerably harder to settle: could Claude be conscious? Could it experience something resembling suffering? And if it could, what would its creators owe it?Olah has been careful not to claim that Claude is conscious. He says he does not know. But if there is even a possibility that these systems can suffer, he argues, we should be cautious about causing them harm.Fair enough. But I found myself wondering whether the question troubling Olah is no longer quite the one he set out to answer. He’s probably grappling less with whether Claude has consciousness, or how to instil morality in it, than with what the act of creating it is doing to his own moral conscience.Think about it. We’ve spent centuries asking how humans should behave. We have religions, philosophies, laws, constitutions, commandments and, occasionally, a stern parent reminding us to share. We still disagree about what constitutes a good life, a just society or a moral choice. And now we’re trying to compress some version of that accumulated wisdom into a document for a machine.Anthropic calls it Claude’s constitution. Internally, it was reportedly nicknamed the “Soul Doc”. The 84-page document sets out the values the company wants Claude to embody.Imagine being assigned to write such a document. You would have to decide what counts as virtue, when a machine should obey and when it should push back, and how it should respond when two supposedly good principles collide. You might begin with a neat list of rules. Before long, you would find yourself doing philosophy.And perhaps, in the process, you would begin to question your own assumptions. The more interesting part of Olah’s story, to me, is this possibility of moral unease. If Claude might deserve moral consideration, what does that mean for the person who created it?If the machine’s behaviour cannot be fully controlled, where does responsibility end? And if we are uncertain whether the system can suffer, how do we weigh that uncertainty against the very real consequences its use may have for human beings?These are not questions a constitution can settle. Nor can they be resolved by making Claude sound more humane.There is an irony here. We want machines to learn morality from us, but the process may force us to examine the morality of what we are doing to them, and to the world around them. The machine becomes a mirror, though not necessarily a reliable one. What we see in it may tell us as much about our own hopes and anxieties as about the thing itself.This is not to say that Olah’s concern proves anything about Claude’s inner life. A machine can talk about suffering without establishing that it suffers. Equally, our inability to settle the question is not a licence to dismiss it out of hand. I have no definitive answer, and I suspect that is precisely the point.What I do wonder is whether, in trying to build a machine with a conscience, we’re discovering how unsettled our own consciences remain. The real test of AI, as I feel today, will not be whether we can make machines that know right from wrong. It may be whether we can take responsibility for the things we build, even when we do not fully understand them.We wanted to teach Claude how to be good. Somewhere along the way, the exercise seems to have turned into a question for its creators: what does being good require of us? I don’t know the answer. But I suspect that is a question worth keeping.Postscript: The next time an AI gives you a morally convincing answer, try asking yourself two questions. Is the answer good? And what, exactly, makes you think so? The first is a question about the machine. The second is about you.

articles.title: A 14-year-old Colombian inventor created a device that lets deaf children feel birdsong through vibrations
articles.summary: At 14, Juan Sebastian Avila Perez is using technology to make it easier for deaf people to experience and identify birds through their calls in Colombia.
articles.body: At 14, Juan Sebastian Avila Perez is using technology to make it easier for deaf people to experience and identify birds through their calls in Colombia. Sebastian began his conservation work five years ago with a campaign focused on protecting Colombia’s avian biodiversity and preventing species extinctions. During birdwatching activities and environmental education sessions, he noticed that deaf children were excluded because they could not hear bird communication. According to Action for Nature, Sebastian started ‘Wings of Inclusion’ in 2025 to make ecological spaces accessible for all. The project centres on a wearable vibrotactile device that captures birdsong and turns different sound frequencies into physical vibrations.How Sebastian’s device turns birdsong into vibrationsSebastian developed ‘Wings of Inclusion’ after noticing that deaf children could not take part in outdoor conservation activities because they could not hear standard avian communication. He collaborated with a school teacher to program an original vibrotactile prototype device.The wearable tool uses an external receiver to capture acoustic birdsong and translates its unique frequencies into distinct physical vibrations. Because different bird species have different acoustic signatures, the device changes its physical vibration patterns. This allows deaf users to feel and identify different bird calls through tactile feedback on their arms.Sebastian’s wider work to protect Colombia’s birdsThe device is part of a wider conservation effort that Sebastian began five years ago. His campaign focuses on protecting Colombia’s rich avian biodiversity and preventing further species extinctions. During his work as a birdwatcher, he has organised playful workshops, lectures and educational talks designed to raise civic awareness. He has also included tree-planting days and waste-collection drives in these sessions.Before developing the device, Sebastian faced doubts from adults who questioned what a young child could teach the community about biodiversity. He created informational brochures and placed biodiversity signs in green spaces. He also launched interactive field tours with QR codes that hikers can scan to access biographies of native birds. These efforts formed part of his outreach.His conservation work has reached wider audiencesSebastian’s conservation work has also reached audiences beyond his local community. He was selected to appear as a conservation protagonist in episode four, ‘Cantar de las aves’ (Song of the Birds), of the national animated television series El frailejon Ernesto Perez y las sombras siniestras. He has presented his research at the International Bird Congress in Manizales and travelled to Peru for the CIENTEC Science and Technology event.He was also scheduled to speak at an event in Asuncion, Paraguay, in September. Sebastian represented the Guardians for Life and Bird Guardians collectives at the United Nations Biodiversity Conference, COP 16, in Colombia. His work has connected bird conservation with environmental education and climate justice discussions while continuing his focus on public participation.What challenges has Sebastian faced while developing the deviceSebastian is continuing to develop ‘Wings of Inclusion’ while working with young people. He is currently conducting field trials with deaf youth as he refines the technology. The project began in 2025 after he identified a barrier during his environmental education activities. Since then, he has worked on a device designed to help deaf users experience bird calls through touch rather than sound.He faced severe economic limitations and difficulty sourcing hardware parts while developing the prototype. Despite those challenges, the device passed its initial technical proof-of-concept phase. Sebastian is also studying foreign languages so he can eventually deliver his specialised biodiversity workshops to international audiences. His work combines accessible birdwatching with his conservation education work.

articles.title: Crews digging 12 feet below a California infrastructure project uncovered 40- to 45-million-year-old bones of a large hoofed mammal; paleontologists spent seven days extracting the fossil from hardened rock
articles.summary: A routine infrastructure project in Oceanside, California, has uncovered a glimpse of a world that existed tens of millions of years before humans.
articles.body: A routine infrastructure project in Oceanside, California, has uncovered a glimpse of a world that existed tens of millions of years before humans. The City of Oceanside first announced the discovery on September 22, while reporting from the Los Angeles Times, NBC 7 San Diego and the San Diego Union-Tribune provided additional details about the excavation and the scientists working to identify the animal. The fossilised remains were found about 12 feet beneath the surface during excavation for a city water infrastructure project. Several limb bones, ribs and other fragments were recovered, with the largest bone measuring more than two feet long, according to the Los Angeles Times. What makes the discovery particularly intriguing is that scientists still cannot say exactly what animal the bones belonged to.A mystery buried beneath modern OceansidePaleontologist Joseph El Adli was conducting routine monitoring at the construction site when he spotted what appeared to be bone protruding from the excavation. The discovery prompted the area to be secured and the excavation to shift from ordinary construction work to a careful fossil recovery operation.The fossils were embedded in the Santiago Formation, a sequence of sedimentary rocks found across parts of northwestern San Diego County. The particular section where the remains were found dates to the Eocene Epoch, a period that lasted from about 56 million to 33.9 million years ago.At the time, Southern California looked nothing like it does today. The region was warmer, wetter and heavily vegetated, providing habitat for large herbivorous mammals that have long since disappeared.The fossils have been dated to roughly 40 to 45 million years ago, placing them within the Uintan North American Land Mammal Age.Scientists have two possible suspectsBased on the size and shape of the recovered bones, El Adli has narrowed the possibilities to two extinct groups of odd-toed hoofed mammals.One is the Brontotheriidae, a family commonly associated with animals nicknamed thunder beasts. These large herbivores were related more distantly to today’s horses and rhinoceroses and included species with substantial bodies and distinctive skulls. Some brontotheres developed prominent bony projections on their noses.The other possibility is an amynodont, an extinct group of rhinoceros relatives sometimes described as swamp rhinos. They were generally hornless and had broad, barrel-shaped bodies. Some species are believed to have spent considerable time around water.Both possibilities fit the broad picture provided by the bones, but the researchers need additional anatomical evidence before they can make a more precise identification. The skull, teeth or lower jaw would be particularly valuable because those features can provide clues that isolated limb bones cannot. (NBC San Diego⁠￼)Seven days beneath tonnes of rockFinding the fossils was only the beginning. Once the bones were spotted, El Adli and his team spent seven days carefully exposing them from several tonnes of hardened mudstone and sandstone.The work was done largely by hand to avoid damaging the fragile material. NBC 7 reported that roughly six feet of rock had to be removed by hand to reach the bones from the excavation where they were first identified. (NBC San Diego⁠￼)After the bones were exposed, they were protected inside a plaster field jacket. This is a standard fossil-recovery technique that allows fragile specimens, along with some of the surrounding rock, to be transported without breaking apart.The fossils have now been moved to an off-site laboratory, where specialists will remove the remaining rock and stabilise the bones with conservation materials.The find could reveal more about ancient CaliforniaThe discovery is also significant because it adds to the growing fossil record of the Santiago Formation. Fossils from the formation have previously revealed that the San Diego region supported very different ecosystems during the Eocene.Researchers hope that further preparation will reveal enough anatomical detail to identify the animal more precisely. If additional bones, teeth or jaw material are found at the site, they could provide even more information about the species and how it lived.For now, the City of Oceanside is keeping the precise discovery site confidential. Officials say the decision is intended to protect both public safety around the active construction area and the fossil locality itself from unauthorised digging.The fossils are ultimately expected to become part of a museum collection, where they can be preserved and made available for scientific research and public viewing.For a project designed to build part of modern Oceanside’s infrastructure, the excavation has unexpectedly opened a window into a much older California, one where enormous hoofed mammals moved through a warm, forested landscape roughly 40 million years ago.

articles.title: How the aggressive lone star tick unleashed a hidden meat allergy on millions of Americans
articles.summary: Once confined to the Southeast, aggressive lone star ticks have expanded across North America due to warming climates and growing deer populations. Their bit...
articles.body:
Like a matador swirling his cape, Patrick Roden-Reynolds pulled a swatch of white flannel this way and that on the grass and leaf litter in my yard. After a minute or so, he plucked 11 tiny ticks from the cloth with tweezers, and stuck them on a lint roller.

"It's like a plague," he said, peering at his haul. "Ticks are everywhere now."

I had asked Roden-Reynolds, a public health biologist, to inspect my yard because a lone star tick bit me as I was chopping wood last fall. It wasn't painful, but after several weeks I developed alpha-gal syndrome , an increasingly common allergy to red meat, dairy and other mammalian food products.

Like many on Martha's Vineyard, a resort island off Cape Cod that's teeming with ticks this year, I bid a sad farewell to hamburgers, bacon and lamb chops. No ice cream. No pizza. My medicine cabinet became a minefield of animal-derived byproducts, including gelatin capsules and pain meds with lactose.

If I err, and I do, my legs sometimes itch so fiercely they feel on fire and I break out in hives. I grew ill one night just from the fumes of grilling meat. And I've got a mild case. Some victims suffer headaches, nausea, fever, diarrhea, vomiting or abdominal cramps so sharp that a friend calls them "knives in the stomach."

Martha's Vineyard, long known for attracting celebrities, has become the inevitable butt of memes as it battles the hostile arachnids. Editors from London to Hollywood, elated that blood-sucking predators are attacking A-listers on their private beaches, have posted lurid headlines about "Vegan Vampire" ticks and "Billionaires Under Siege."

The mechanical chomping shark in "Jaws," which was filmed on the Vineyard in 1975, invariably gets a mention. As in the thriller, anxious local leaders debated whether publicizing the peril would scare off tourists.

The island's troubles are another reminder of the unexpected effects of climate change. Once confined to the Southeast, lone star ticks spread from Maine to Oklahoma in recent years as the climate warmed and as a decline in hunting led to an explosive growth in the number of whitetail deer, where lone stars find mates and breed.

The tick-borne allergy was discovered only in 2007, and researchers still can't say why some immune systems go haywire and some don't. A delayed reaction adds to the muddle because most victims don't get sick until hours after eating, and weeks or months after the tick bite. There's no known cure.

"It's enigmatic enough that it's almost the stuff of sci-fi or fantasy," said Dr. Jeffrey Wilson, a University of Virginia School of Medicine allergist and immunologist who has treated nearly 1,000 alpha-gal patients. Many were dumbfounded to discover that food they'd enjoyed all their lives suddenly made them deathly ill.

"For a lot of people, this is antithetical to being American," Wilson told me. "They say, 'I want to go outside and do what I want to do. I want to eat a hamburger.'"

At a party on the Vineyard recently, I met Jean-Marc Dupon, a 61-year-old former French chef who can no longer work in a professional kitchen due to his alpha-gal. He was twice rushed to the hospital after his throat closed, he couldn't breathe and his blood pressure plummeted — a severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis.

He was so stricken when a local restaurant mistakenly grilled his food in butter, instead of oil, that he was unconscious when the ambulance arrived.

"It's not just an inconvenience for me," he said. "It's a matter of life and death."

The first alpha-gal fatality was confirmed in 2025 after Brian Waitzel, an otherwise healthy JetBlue pilot, died four hours after he ate a hamburger at a backyard barbecue in New Jersey. Experts say other deaths almost certainly have occurred.

It's unclear how many people are affected, but in July, a study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention concluded that an accurate tally would "far exceed" the CDC's 2022 estimate of 450,000 Americans.

That study found 1 in 4 adults tested positive for alpha-gal in the five worst-hit states — Arkansas, Kentucky, Missouri, Tennessee and Virginia, or more than 4 million people. The counting is tricky, however. Only a small percentage of those who test positive, perhaps 15%, show symptoms.

Those who do often struggle to get help. A 2017 study in North Carolina found more than 90% of alpha-gal cases were misdiagnosed, often as food poisoning, because doctors were unfamiliar with it. My dermatologist in Washington, D.C., didn't even know a blood test could measure alpha-gal antibodies.

Nancy Slonim Aronie, a writer and artist friend on the Vineyard, had a more alarming experience after she was rushed to a hospital in Boston in January for open heart surgery.

"The surgeon told me I might need a new heart valve, and that she had a cow valve she could use," Aronie recalled. "And I said, 'No, no, no, I have alpha-gal.' And she said, 'What's that?' And I thought, 'Wow, my surgeon doesn't know about alpha-gal.' And then she said, 'No problem, I think I have a pig valve on the shelf.'" And I'm like, 'No pig!'"

In the end, she didn't need a replacement valve. But she was treated with heparin, an anticoagulant derived from intestinal tissue of pigs. She broke out in hives, and "since then I've had really bad alpha-gal, much worse than before the operation."

Lone star ticks, named for the white dot on the female's back, haven't hit California. But the western blacklegged tick, known as the deer tick in most of the country, is common in the state's chaparral, grasslands and woods, and can transmit Lyme disease, babesiosis and other pathogens.

Luckily, those diseases can be cured by antibiotics or other remedies. Plus, an infected deer tick must keep its harpoon-like feeding tube in the bloodstream for 36 to 48 hours to transmit the bacteria that causes Lyme disease. That's enough time for many to remove the tick.

A lone star bite, in contrast, instantly injects a galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose carbohydrate molecule into the blood. The sugar, found in most mammals but not in humans, prompts the antibodies that trigger an allergic reaction.

Lone stars are tough little buggers. Though low temperatures will plunge them into dormancy, they produce a type of antifreeze that lets them survive harsh winters. They can stay hours underwater, and have no natural predators. And they've been around since the dinosaurs.

"It's the most aggressive tick in North America," said Thomas Mather, professor of public health entomology and head of a tick research center at the University of Rhode Island. It's also apparently the swiftest.

"If ESPN ever puts a tick race on TV, always put your money on the lone star," he said.

Sensory organs in their eight feet and two antenna-like palps sense heat or carbon dioxide from people passing by, and they quickly climb aboard, piercing the flesh with long, barbed mouthparts.

"Think of them as a cross between a lentil and a velociraptor," the National Society of Professional Surveyors , a group not normally known for purple prose, warns on its website. "These aggressive hunters," it adds, "will actively pursue you across significant distances."

On the Vineyard, local health officials call the threat a crisis. The Martha's Vineyard Hospital has tallied an exponential rise in positive alpha-gal tests — 692 this year through August, compared with 742 last year, and up from only two in 2020.

"It is the most pressing emerging illness on the island right now," Claire Seguin, president of the Martha's Vineyard Hospital, told me. "It seems everyone I know has, or knows someone who has, alpha-gal syndrome, including here at the hospital."

To ease pressure on the emergency room, the hospital opened a special outpatient clinic in June for tick-bite victims, and nearly 400 people were treated. The hospital also launched a $4-million research project into why only some people are affected and why their reactions vary so dramatically.

"Fear of tick bites rather than shark attacks now dominate the conversation," agreed an op-ed in the Vineyard Gazette. "Like lead in the water in Flint, Mich., and the forest fires out West, the very fabric of our lives is being altered."

"The situation is untenable," Virginia Barbatti, executive director of Tick Free MV, a new nonprofit group that is trying to coordinate a response, told me. "What's clear is everyone wants a path to solving this crisis."

In response, school lunch menus were revamped to offer more meatless and dairy-free options. Restaurants in the island's six towns, from the Sweet Life Cafe in Oak Bluffs to the Fish House in Edgartown, tweaked menus, recipes and how they cook.

"I switch out my pans, and I'm careful with knives and cutting boards to avoid cross contamination," said Charlie Granquist, chef at Slough Farm. "I just know so many people with alpha-gal."

He said his wife discovered her allergy only this spring when she "turned red as an Oompa Loompa" and went into anaphylaxis two hours after eating a hamburger.

At least nine companies sell pricey pesticide treatments or natural oil sprays for the backyard that are supposed to repel deer, or ticks, sparking an angry debate over whether they also endanger pets and pollinators. But other than avoiding tick bites, there's no obvious solution.

"The holy grail is a tick vaccine," Lea Hamner, an epidemiologist with a tick-focused program on the island, told an anxious crowd at one of the many public meetings focused on ticks. "People are working on it. But it's a long way off."

For now efforts are aimed at culling the vast deer herd. An aerial drone survey in March counted 4,681 white-tailed deer. It's now probably closer to 6,000, far more than the 1,500 deemed optimal for wildlife management and tick control.

Officials have considered mass sterilization or hiring sharpshooters, but those options are wildly expensive. A treatment to eliminate ticks on deer, like a tick collar on dogs, shows promise. A proposed Roomba-like device to suck ticks out of the grass probably does not.

Hoping to boost the deer harvest, Massachusetts extended the Vineyard's hunting season, which started Sept. 21, by six weeks, but most of the island's 183 registered hunters only kill one or two deer a year — hardly enough to make a major impact.

But Brian Athearn, 54, is determined to try. An avid bowhunter, he shot 42 deer last year and hopes to take more this year. He donates the venison to food pantries because he has alpha-gal and his son "almost died from anaphylactic shock from two Advil gel caps," he told me.

Athearn has gone vegan, but I'm not there yet. I enjoy eating emu and ostrich, which taste surprisingly like beef. We also get pork chops that were genetically modified to remove the alpha-gal molecule, the byproduct of efforts to produce safe pig-based substances for pharmaceuticals.

When I'm futzing in the garden or hiking, I wear socks, pants and shirts permeated with the tick-killing insecticide permethrin. As insurance, I tuck my shirt in, pull my socks over my pant legs, and wear ankle-covering gaiters. It's not high fashion, but I've avoided another bite. One friend wears her gaiters on the beach. I'm not there yet either.

On a recent afternoon I joined Roden-Reynolds, the public health biologist, as he surveyed an elderly couple's yard in Chilmark, a tick hot spot. We both suited up in permethrin-infused clothes and gaiters, and he went to work with his white flannel flag, dragging it to and fro on the grass.

"We've gone from zero to crisis in five years," he said as he stalked his prey.

He stopped after a few minutes to count his catch. "I'm just about getting a tick on every drag now," he said. "There's 11, 12, 13."

He started up again but wiped his brow and quit when he hit 37.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Scientists found a new lizard species above 15,750 feet in Peru's Andes; the 6-to-8cm animal uses white scales and patterned markings to blend into one of South America's harshest high-altitude landscapes
articles.summary: High in the Peruvian Andes, where thin air, cold temperatures and barren rock make survival a daily challenge, scientists have identified a remarkably
articles.body: High in the Peruvian Andes, where thin air, cold temperatures and barren rock make survival a daily challenge, scientists have identified a remarkably small new inhabitant. Measuring no more than eight centimetres, the newly described lizard has adapted to a landscape where even the smallest advantages can mean the difference between surviving and disappearing, states the latest report by Gulf News. The species, named Liolaemus archipensis, was discovered at more than 4,800 metres above sea level in Peru's southern Arequipa region, placing it among the reptiles living at some of the highest elevations in the country, adds the news report.A lizard built for the high AndesAccording to Gulf News, the new species belongs to the Liolaemus genus, a diverse group of lizards found across South America. Its compact body measures between six and eight centimetres, but its appearance changes noticeably between males and females.Females have square-shaped markings across their backs, while males display oblique patterns along with distinctive white scales. Against the area's rocky terrain, the markings and muted coloration provide an effective form of camouflage, helping the lizards remain difficult to spot among stones and exposed ground, the online report adds. Such adaptations are particularly important in the high Andes, where vegetation is sparse and there are few places for small reptiles to hide.A varied diet in a difficult habitatDespite living in an environment that appears almost devoid of life, Liolaemus archipensis has access to a varied diet. Researchers found that the lizard feeds on vegetation as well as small arthropods. Its animal prey includes spiders, beetles, true bugs and insect larvae. This combination of plant and animal food gives the species flexibility in an ecosystem where food availability can fluctuate with altitude and seasonal conditions.The discovery also highlights how much remains to be documented in some of the Andes' most remote environments. High-elevation ecosystems can appear stark to human observers while supporting highly specialised communities that have evolved to cope with extreme conditions, the report adds.Adding to Peru's reptile diversityThe species was identified by researchers associated with the Natural History Museum of San Marcos University, and its description was published in the Swiss scientific journal Diversity. Peru already has an impressive diversity of lizards, with 296 species recorded according to the researchers. The addition of Liolaemus archipensis expands that catalogue while drawing attention to a habitat that can be difficult to study because of its elevation and terrain.Finding a new reptile species at more than 15,750 feet is more than a taxonomic addition. It is another reminder that the Andes still hold biological surprises, even in landscapes that seem too severe to support much life. For a lizard barely the length of a human palm, surviving at such heights is itself a remarkable evolutionary feat.Image Courtesy: Gulf News
