articles.title: In 2020, researchers tested chicken-feather waste as an asphalt modifier; at 2%, the feather blend performed comparably to a synthetic paving polymer and showed better storage stability in lab tests
articles.summary: Could one of the food industry's most overlooked leftovers get a second life beneath our wheels?
articles.body: Could one of the food industry's most overlooked leftovers get a second life beneath our wheels? Chicken feathers are often considered a waste product after poultry processing, but they’ve emerged as an unlikely candidate for improving asphalt. According to research titled 'Influence of chicken feather on the rheological properties and performance of modified asphalts' published in 2020, under Construction and Building Materials, tiny particles made from discarded feathers could replace or supplement synthetic materials traditionally used to reinforce road surfaces. According to a release shared by Science Direct, the results were promising. Asphalt with 2% chicken-feather particles had performance similar to that of a blend of asphalt containing the same amount of synthetic styrene-butadiene-styrene (SBS) polymer. More importantly the feather-modified mixture exhibited better storage stability in laboratory tests. Scroll down to read the details.Poultry waste converted into road materialAsphalt is one of the most used materials in infrastructure as the binder component of roads, and also for waterproofing and protective coatings. But traditional asphalt has its drawbacks. Pavement deteriorates, through rutting, cracking and fatigue, due to heavy traffic, repeated loading and temperature and environmental variations. To address these issues, engineers often add polymers and other modifiers to enhance the material’s elasticity, strength, flexibility and resistance to deformation. SBS is one of the most tried and true.But the growing volume of organic and solid waste has driven researchers to look for alternatives which can serve for a technical purpose and at the same time reduce the pressure on disposal. Chicken feathers are of special interest because they are produced in large quantities by the poultry industry, but their uses in high-value applications are rather limited, the study published by Science Direct states.Why feathers caught the attention of the researchersThis study investigated the use of chicken-feather bioparticles (CFBP) as an asphalt modifier. Blends containing 2%, 4% and 6% by weight of feather particles were prepared and their behavior compared to that of asphalt modified with SBS.The team looked at the rheological properties, which are useful in showing how asphalt behaves under stress, temperature and loading over time. The tests looked at things like complex modulus, elastic modulus, viscous modulus and phase angle.These properties are important as roads should bear the repeated pressure without permanent deformation. A more pronounced elastic response can help asphalt to bounce back after loading and changes in stiffness and phase behavior can impact on its resistance to rutting and other types of damage.You could taste the 2% mixThe study also states that the most striking comparison to the synthetic polymer blend was obtained with the 2% chicken feather mixture. The rheological behavior was found to be similar to that of an asphalt modified with 2% SBS suggesting that feathers derived material can have a similar modifying role at relatively low concentrations.The feather-based mixture also demonstrated a significant benefit during storage. In polymer-modified asphalts, phase separation may occur when the components are not compatible enough. The polymer-rich and asphalt-rich portions can separate over time, causing problems with handling, consistency and pavement performance.In laboratory tests, 2% chicken feather blend exhibited better storage stability than the corresponding SBS modified blend.A potential sustainability benefitThe research study is significant not only for laboratory measurements. Replacing some of the synthetic modifiers in asphalt with waste-derived material could provide a pathway to transform poultry waste into a useful construction resource. It may also reduce reliance on petroleum-derived synthetic polymers and potentially reduce the cost of materials . At the same time, using feathers that otherwise would be considered waste could help solve an environmental problem associated with large-scale poultry production, it states.That doesn’t mean feather-modified asphalt is ready to replace traditional road materials everyplace. The findings are based on laboratory work and further research is needed to understand how the mixtures behave under real traffic, weather and long-term aging conditions.But the study points to a broader change in construction research: waste does not need to be waste. Discarded tires, industrial by-products and agricultural residues are among the materials once considered difficult to dispose of and now increasingly being explored as ingredients for more resource-efficient infrastructure. The road ahead could be surprisingly useful for something as mundane as a chicken feather.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: Scientists re-examined 46 skulls excavated from Egypt’s First Dynasty royal cemetery in the 1920s; 18 showed significant cranial trauma, adding new forensic evidence for retainer sacrifice about 5,000 years ago
articles.summary: Researchers have found new evidence that some people buried around the tombs of Egypt’s First Dynasty kings may have been deliberately killed after the
articles.body: Researchers have found new evidence that some people buried around the tombs of Egypt’s First Dynasty kings may have been deliberately killed after the rulers died. The finding published in journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, comes from a fresh examination of 46 skulls excavated from a royal cemetery at Abydos in the 1920s.The remains were originally excavated by British archaeologist Flinders Petrie. He had suspected that the large number of people buried around the royal tombs could be evidence of retainer sacrifice. In this practice, people close to a ruler were killed after the ruler’s death so they could continue serving the ruler in the afterlife.However, Petrie had not found clear evidence of fatal injuries on the bones. That left the cause of death uncertain for decades. The new examination of preserved skulls uses modern forensic knowledge and identified significant cranial trauma in 18 of the 46 skulls studied.According to the research, at least 39% of the people represented by the examined skulls may have been deliberately killed by blows to the head. The findings provide new forensic evidence supporting the possibility that retainer sacrifice took place at Abydos about 5,000 years ago.The burials around royal tombsThe funerary complexes at Abydos were built around 3000 BCE by the first kings of a unified Egypt. Along with the royal tombs, the complexes included chamber tombs and enclosures that were probably used for funerary rituals. There were also many subsidiary burials around the tombs and enclosures.The subsidiary graves were arranged in rows, with some royal tombs surrounded by hundreds of burials. According to Dr Roselyn Campbell, a bioarchaeologist and Egyptologist at Purdue University, each burial was a simple chamber, and some people were buried with a basic coffin.Many graves contained a small number of grave goods, including ceramic vessels, copper tools, projectile points and small ivory figurines. Some of the graves also had markers carrying names or official titles. Campbell says these titles mostly referred to lower- or mid-level officials and artisans.The large number of burials led Petrie to question whether all the deaths could have happened naturally. The clustering of the graves around royal tombs also raised the possibility that these people had died at the same time as the rulers they were associated with.Why Petrie suspected mass sacrificeRetainer sacrifice refers to the killing of people close to a ruler when the ruler dies. The belief behind the practice in some cultures was that those people would continue serving the ruler after death.But the practice could also serve as a display of the ruler’s power. Campbell said some retainers may have volunteered to die because they believed it could bring them eternal life or honour, while others could have been selected or forced.The Abydos burials had features that made Petrie suspect such a practice. However, the absence of obvious lethal injuries meant that there was no direct physical evidence to prove that the people had been killed.Campbell, from Purdue University, decided to revisit the surviving remains using modern forensic knowledge. She searched for material from Petrie’s excavations and found 46 skulls in the Duckworth Collection at the University of Cambridge.Modern forensics find injuriesThe re-examination identified significant cranial trauma in 18 of the 46 skulls. The injuries included linear fractures, which appear as lines or breaks in the skull.Campbell said Petrie appears to have interpreted some of these injuries as damage caused naturally after death. Modern forensic methods, however, allow researchers to recognise them as perimortem injuries, meaning injuries that occurred around the time of death.“The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death,” Campbell said.Some of the 18 skulls also showed evidence of sharp-force trauma. One individual had a chopping injury around the eye.The researchers cannot determine exactly how the injuries were inflicted. Egyptian kings are often shown using a mace to strike enemies, but the people buried around these royal tombs were not enemies. A mace would also be expected to cause depressed fractures, rather than the linear fractures found on these skulls.Linear fractures can be caused by a flat, wide weapon or by a fall. However, a fall powerful enough to cause such a fracture would probably also have broken other bones. Such injuries should have been visible in Petrie’s photographs or mentioned in his notes, according to the research.Cause of death uncertain for othersThe findings do not explain what happened to all the people buried around the royal tombs. Some may have died naturally. Others may have been killed in ways that did not leave clear marks on the skeleton.For example, asphyxiation may not leave skeletal evidence. Other forms of violence may also only be identified by examining the complete skeletons rather than the skulls alone.Most of the remains excavated by Petrie were reburied, while he kept some skulls, including those later sent to the UK. This means researchers now have only an incomplete sample of the people buried at the site.Campbell said further examination of the bodies could provide more information about how these individuals died. “If I had unlimited resources, I would love to figure out where the bodies of these individuals might be and analyze them,” she said.

articles.title: Oklahoma’s Ames crater was linked to a 470-million-year-old event; zircon dating suggests it may be nearly 370 million years old, near an extinction
articles.summary: For decades, scientists linked Oklahoma’s Ames impact structure to a meteor event that swept across Earth nearly 470 million years ago.
articles.body: For decades, scientists linked Oklahoma’s Ames impact structure to a meteor event that swept across Earth nearly 470 million years ago. According to research published in Meteoritics & Planetary Science titled ‘The Ames impact structure, Oklahoma: New radioisotopic constraints and implications for North American impact chronology’, new evidence points to a very different timeline. By dating zircon from impact-melted granite, researchers may have found a distinct group of grains with an age of nearly 370 million years, suggesting the crater formed during the Late Devonian. That would place the impact close to the Frasnian-Famennian boundary and the Upper Kellwasser Crisis, a major extinction event.How did new dating place the Ames impact near a major extinctionThe Ames impact structure lies beneath Ames, Oklahoma, with an outer rim measuring 14-16 km in diameter. It was previously considered one of the largest impact structures associated with the Ordovician Meteor Event, which began about 466-468 million years ago. This connection was based on conodonts and moulds identified in material filling the crater.To test the age of the impact, researchers used radioisotopic dating on zircon and plagioclase from impacted granite. The youngest zircon population had a weighted mean age of nearly 370 million years.The researchers interpret this as a maximum age for the impact event. If correct, this would place the Ames impact in the Late Devonian rather than the Ordovician, changing its position in North American impact chronology.How did zircon dating reveal the age of the Ames impactResearchers analysed zircon from the impact-melt portion of the Ames structure using secondary ion mass spectrometry and laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry. They made 37 measurements.The youngest zircon dates formed a distinct population. 10 of the 11 analyses gave a weighted mean age of nearly 370 million years after one statistical outlier was excluded. Most zircons, including the youngest Devonian-age grains, retained their primary oscillatory zoning and showed no signs of deformation.Two zircons displayed impact-related textures, including low-angle grain boundaries within microcracks and granular zircon arrays crossing their growth zoning.Why did the earlier fossil evidence place the Ames impact in the OrdovicianThe earlier Ordovician age for Ames came from Middle Ordovician conodonts and moulds found in the Crater Shale. The study says this age was based on only four small chips and that the Crater Shale has poorly understood and debated stratigraphic relationships.The researchers propose that the impact excavated Middle to Upper Ordovician Simpson Group strata and disrupted fossil-bearing sediments. Those materials could then have been redeposited inside the crater during resurge and tsunami backwash.Under this interpretation, the conodonts came from older rocks struck by the impact and were later deposited inside the crater. Rapid redeposition and burial inside the crater may also have helped preserve the delicate fossil remains.Ames impact dates to the period of the Late Devonian extinctionThe nearly 370-million-year-old zircon age falls close to the Frasnian-Famennian boundary, which marks the Upper Kellwasser Crisis, an extinction event. The Ames result falls within the broader Middle to Late Devonian window of other North American impacts, though some are somewhat older. The paper lists Flynn Creek in Tennessee at about 382 million years, Nicholson Lake in Canada at about 385 million years, and the Alamo impact-related deposits in Nevada at 355-382 million years.If the zircon interpretation is correct, the Ames impact may provide additional evidence for one or more large bolide impacts during the Late Devonian. The researchers say this could inform discussions about links between extraterrestrial impacts and environmental disturbances associated with the Frasnian-Famennian mass extinction.

articles.title: Florida's Burmese pythons are carrying three previously unknown RNA viruses; scientists are investigating whether they could reach native snakes
articles.summary: Burmese pythons in Florida's Everglades are carrying three previously unknown RNA viruses, raising questions about whether viruses harboured by the
articles.body: Burmese pythons in Florida's Everglades are carrying three previously unknown RNA viruses, raising questions about whether viruses harboured by the invasive snakes could eventually affect native wildlife. A study published in the Journal of Virology examined 40 Burmese pythons captured in and around the site of a 2020 disease outbreak among eastern mudsnakes. Researchers did not find the ferlavirus linked to that outbreak in the pythons, but instead identified three previously undescribed viruses: an alphavirus, a hepacivirus and an arterivirus. They also detected a previously characterised serpentovirus. While the findings expand knowledge of viruses carried by invasive reptiles, researchers say further work is needed to determine whether any of these viruses can infect native snakes.Florida’s Burmese pythons found carrying new RNA virusesThe research began after an outbreak among eastern mudsnakes in the Greater Everglades Ecosystem during November and December 2020. Some affected snakes were found writhing on riverbanks with frothy oral discharge, while examinations revealed necrotising enteritis and pulmonary oedema. Scientists isolated a reptilian ferlavirus from the sick mudsnakes. Ferlaviruses are known to cause serious and sometimes fatal disease in snakes kept in managed settings, but this was the first recognised outbreak in free-ranging snakes. Because the virus was genetically related to viruses previously found in captive anacondas, researchers investigated whether an invasive constrictor species in the Everglades might be involved in its ecology.Researchers tested 40 Burmese pythonsResearchers collected oral and vent swabs from 40 Burmese pythons captured in and around the outbreak area. None tested positive for the ferlavirus found in the mudsnakes. Instead, RNA sequencing revealed three previously undescribed viruses: Eden alphavirus, Burmese python hepacivirus and Burmese python arterivirus. The researchers also detected Burmese python septoviruses, a group of serpentoviruses previously identified in South Florida's Burmese pythons.Eden alphavirus was found in nearly one-third of pythonsEden alphavirus, or EDEV, belongs to the genus Alphavirus in the family Togaviridae. Researchers detected it in 12 of the 40 pythons, or 30%. Most detections came from vent samples. Only a partial viral sequence was recovered, and attempts to grow the virus in laboratory cell cultures were unsuccessful. EDEV's closest known relatives include Caainguá virus, first identified in mosquito pools in Brazil. The researchers describe EDEV as the first new terrestrial alphavirus detected in the continental US in more than 50 years. However, its ability to cause disease remains unknown, and the study provides no evidence that it infects humans.A new hepacivirus was found in most of the snakesBurmese python hepacivirus, or BuPyHV, was the most frequently detected of the three newly identified viruses. It was found in 26 of the 40 pythons, meaning 65% had detectable viral RNA. The virus belongs to the genus Hepacivirus in the family Flaviviridae and is described by the researchers as the first hepacivirus identified in a snake. Although the genus also includes hepatitis C virus, BuPyHV is genetically distinct, and there is no evidence that it causes hepatitis in humans. Researchers identified an unusually elongated region in its genome and a possible additional protease-related protein whose function remains unknown.The third virus was a previously unknown arterivirusThe third novel virus, provisionally named Burmese python arterivirus or BuPyAV, was detected in four of the 40 pythons, or 10%. It belongs to the family Arteriviridae. Researchers recovered only a short section of its genome, limiting what they could determine about its evolution. Its closest known relative was a greater green snake arterivirus identified in China. The study describes BuPyAV as the first reptilian arterivirus reported from North America. Its ability to cause disease or spread between animals has yet to be established.More than half of the pythons carried multiple virusesThe researchers found that many of the pythons carried more than one virus. Two or three viruses were detected in 23 of the 40 animals, representing 57.5% of the sample. The most common combination was Burmese python hepacivirus and serpentovirus, detected together in nine pythons. Eden alphavirus and hepacivirus were found together in seven. The serpentoviruses identified in the study have previously been associated with respiratory disease in captive snakes. However, detecting viral RNA does not by itself establish that a particular snake was ill because of the virus.Cross-species transmission remains an open questionThe findings do not show that any of the three newly identified viruses have already spread from Burmese pythons to native snakes. Researchers instead identify cross-species transmission as an issue that warrants further investigation. The ferlavirus associated with the 2020 mudsnake outbreak was also absent from the 40 pythons tested, so the study does not establish that Burmese pythons caused or introduced that outbreak. The concern is largely ecological. Burmese pythons occupy the same environment as numerous native species, creating opportunities for pathogens to encounter new hosts. Scientists now need to determine whether the newly identified viruses can infect other snake species, replicate in them or cause disease.Scientists need to determine what the viruses doFinding viral genetic material is only the beginning. Researchers still need to establish how the viruses are transmitted, whether they can replicate in other species and whether they have any measurable effects on snake health or native ecosystems. The study's viral sequences have been deposited in GenBank, providing material for further research. Published online on February 24, 2026, in the Journal of Virology, the study brings attention to the largely unexplored viral diversity associated with invasive Burmese pythons. For now, the evidence points to viral diversity rather than confirmed spread. The three viruses were detected in Burmese pythons, but their ability to move into native snake populations remains unknown.

articles.title: Scientists found a new way to make hydrogen from water using light; the material avoids an expensive metal catalyst and could make clean hydrogen production cheaper
articles.summary: Hydrogen has long carried the promise of becoming a cleaner fuel, but making it sustainably remains one of the biggest challenges.
articles.body: Hydrogen has long carried the promise of becoming a cleaner fuel, but making it sustainably remains one of the biggest challenges. Now, researchers at Oregon State University have developed a new material that uses light to split water and produce hydrogen, opening another possible route to solar-powered fuel production without relying on an expensive metal catalyst. Led by Kyriakos Stylianou of the OSU College of Science, the research centres on a specially designed photocatalyst that can harness light energy to accelerate the chemical reactions needed to generate hydrogen, states the research study published by Science Daily.Turning light into chemical energyAccording to the research, a photocatalyst works much like an ordinary catalyst, speeding up a chemical reaction without being consumed by it. The difference is that light activates the material, pushing it into a higher-energy state and allowing it to drive reactions more efficiently. To do that, the OSU team looked to metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs. They are crystalline porous materials made of metal ions and organic molecules called the linkers. Their structures can be modified at the molecular level, giving researchers considerable control over their chemical and physical properties.The sheer design potential of MOFs is enormous and while scientists have already synthesised nearly 100,000 different structures, hundreds of thousands more have been predicted computationally.An unusual role for sulfurFor the new study, researchers focused on a MOF known as BVR-19. Its distinctive feature is an unusual bond between sulfur atoms within its organic component. When exposed to light, that bond can temporarily break, generating highly reactive sulfur species. These then help capture light energy and move electrons through the material, ultimately supporting the production of hydrogen from water, states the study.This mechanism is significant because the organic component, rather than the metal centre, plays the leading role in the light-driven chemistry. That gives BVR-19 a fundamentally different operating principle from many conventional photocatalytic systems. It also eliminates the need for an additional costly metal catalyst, potentially simplifying the design of future systems aimed at producing hydrogen using sunlight.Made in water, at room temperatureBVR-19 has another feature that could prove valuable for practical applications. The material forms spontaneously in an aqueous solution at room temperature, meaning its production does not require large amounts of energy, the study mentions.That could become important as researchers look beyond laboratory performance and consider the overall energy and environmental cost of producing photocatalytic materials themselves.The green hydrogen challengeHydrogen is already essential to industries ranging from ammonia production and metal refining to plastics manufacturing, and it is increasingly being explored for fuel-cell vehicles and other energy applications. Much of today's hydrogen, however, is produced through methane-steam reforming, a process that releases carbon dioxide. Splitting water using renewable electricity or sunlight offers a cleaner alternative, but the economics remain difficult.Conventional hydrogen production through methane-steam reforming costs roughly $1.50 per kilogram, while green hydrogen can cost around $5 per kilogram. Lowering that gap will require cheaper materials, efficient reactions and less energy-intensive production methods, the study also highlights.A new blueprint for solar fuelThe Oregon State research offers more than a new photocatalyst. By examining how changes to the metal component influence the performance of closely related MOFs, the researchers identified structural clues that can help guide the development of more effective materials. The larger goal is to make solar-powered hydrogen production more efficient and less expensive. BVR-19 remains a research-stage material, and more work will be needed to assess its performance at larger scales and in real-world conditions. But its unusual chemistry offers a promising new direction: using light, water and carefully engineered materials to turn a basic chemical reaction into a potential source of cleaner fuel.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: In 1925, a hydrothermal explosion reshaped Yellowstone’s Biscuit Basin; 101 years later, USGS reconstructed from 1926 letters how a misplaced ‘Black Pearl’ sign shifted the story 1,000 feet from the real geyser
articles.summary: A century-old mystery at Yellowstone’s Biscuit Basin has turned out to be less about a missing geyser and more about a misplaced sign.
articles.body: A century-old mystery at Yellowstone’s Biscuit Basin has turned out to be less about a missing geyser and more about a misplaced sign. In 1925, a hydrothermal explosion dramatically altered part of the basin, but because nobody witnessed the event, the details were later pieced together from observations and correspondence. One particularly confusing clue was a “Black Pearl” sign that ended up about 1,000 feet from the actual geyser it was meant to identify. According to the U.S. Geological Survey’s Yellowstone Volcano Observatory, two letters written in 1926 have now helped reconstruct how the mix-up happened and clarify the history of the area.An explosion that went unnoticedThe 1925 event was relatively small compared with some of Yellowstone’s much larger hydrothermal explosions, but it still changed the landscape around Biscuit Basin. According to the USGS, the explosion happened near the Firehole River and tore through the area’s fragile sinter crust. It likely created or enlarged a new thermal pool near Black Diamond Pool.One major problem for anyone trying to document what happened was that nobody saw the explosion when it occurred. By the time people examined the area, they had to rely on what the landscape looked like afterward. That made identifying and naming the new thermal features more difficult.Where the Black Pearl confusion beganThe trouble centred on a sign. Visitors found a weathered sign carrying the name “Black Pearl” close to the area affected by the explosion. The problem was that the feature the sign appeared to identify could not be found there. The real Black Pearl Geyser was located roughly 1,000 feet to the west.The geyser itself was distinctive. It was known for dark, pearl-like spheres of sinter that covered its surface. Meanwhile, the thermal features closer to Black Diamond Pool had their own names. Wall Pool was to the west, while Black Opal Pool was to the east. At some point, the Black Pearl sign had apparently been moved, creating the impression that a different thermal feature was the famous geyser.Two letters helped solve the mysteryThe mix-up might have remained a minor historical curiosity if not for correspondence preserved in Yellowstone’s archives. In a letter dated August 15, 1926, J. R. Van Pelt, a ranger at Old Faithful, wrote to J. E. Haynes, acting director of the Yellowstone Park Museum. Van Pelt explained the situation surrounding the previous year's explosion and the misplaced sign.Another letter followed on August 26, 1926. Haynes wrote back to Van Pelt, confirming that some of the signage was out of position and asking that the signs be returned to their appropriate locations. The exchange included discussions involving park officials, painters and earlier naming practices elsewhere in Yellowstone. What might have seemed like routine administrative correspondence a century ago has now become an important piece of evidence for reconstructing the story.Why a misplaced sign matteredAt first glance, getting a sign wrong by 1,000 feet may sound like a small mistake. In Yellowstone, however, names and locations are closely tied to the geological record. Thermal features can change, disappear, become dormant or appear in new forms. A name attached to the wrong pool can therefore make it difficult for later visitors and researchers to understand which feature historical records were describing. The 1925 explosion was already difficult to document because no one witnessed it. Confusing the names afterward added another layer of uncertainty.The episode also reflects how information was recorded and shared in the early 20th century. There were no modern monitoring systems, digital photographs or instant communication. Details often travelled through handwritten letters and personal observations, leaving plenty of room for misunderstandings.Yellowstone’s hydrothermal landscape keeps changingThe story has gained renewed attention because Biscuit Basin has experienced more recent hydrothermal activity. In July 2024, a hydrothermal explosion occurred at Black Diamond Pool. Such explosions happen when superheated water suddenly turns to steam, breaking apart the rock that confines it. They can leave behind craters, scattered debris and major changes to the surrounding landscape.The area has continued to be monitored. The Yellowstone Volcano Observatory has installed equipment at Biscuit Basin to create a better record of ongoing and future activity. That modern monitoring is a sharp contrast with what happened in 1925. Scientists now have instruments and cameras that can capture changes as they occur rather than relying mainly on observations made afterward.A small historical error with a bigger lessonThe misplaced Black Pearl sign is ultimately more than an old naming error. It shows how easily the record of a geological event can become blurred when an event is not directly witnessed. The 1926 letters allowed the USGS to separate the actual Black Pearl Geyser from the feature associated with the misplaced sign and reconstruct what happened after the 1925 explosion.More than a century later, the landscape around Biscuit Basin continues to change. But this time, scientists have modern monitoring equipment in place to document those changes, reducing the chances that another geological event will become tangled in a similar mystery.

articles.title: China sigue dando pasos para crear el "sol artificial": el proyecto de fusión nuclear de Hefei sigue quemando etapas
articles.standfirst: El proyecto ubicado en la ciudad de Hefei es gestionado por los Institutos de Ciencias Físicas de Hefei, pertenecientes a la Academia China de Ciencias
articles.summary: El proyecto ubicado en la ciudad de Hefei es gestionado por los Institutos de Ciencias Físicas de Hefei, pertenecientes a la Academia China de Ciencias
articles.body: La ciudad china de Hefei se ha consolidado como la capital mundial de la investigación en fusión nuclear. A través de las instalaciones desarrolladas en sus institutos científicos, el país asiático busca recrear el proceso energético que alimenta a las estrellas para desarrollar una fuente de energía limpia, inagotable y segura. En los últimos años, el buque insignia de este enclave, el reactor Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST) —conocido popularmente como el "sol artificial"—, ha cosechado hitos científicos clave. El dispositivo logró mantener plasma súper caliente a temperaturas superiores a los 100 millones de grados Celsius y batió récords al sostener el confinamiento del plasma durante más de 1.000 segundos. Recientemente, las investigaciones en EAST también han logrado avances trascendentales al desafiar inestabilidades físicas históricas y superar los límites teóricos de densidad en el plasma experimental. Lejos de detenerse en la fase experimental del EAST, el programa científico de Hefei ha dado un salto cualitativo con el desarrollo de su siguiente instalación, el Burning Plasma Experimental Superconducting Tokamak (BEST). La construcción civil y el complejo principal de este nuevo reactor se han completado con éxito, lo que ha permitido iniciar formalmente la fase de montaje e instalación de sus sistemas avanzados. A diferencia de su antecesor, BEST utilizará directamente una mezcla de combustible de deuterio y tritio orientada a demostrar la viabilidad práctica del rendimiento energético neto. En cuanto a la hoja de ruta temporal, la planificación del proyecto BEST fija la finalización de sus obras de ingeniería y el montaje de componentes para finales de 2027. Inmediatamente después, el reactor tiene previsto obtener su primer plasma operativo, lo que lo convertirá en la instalación más avanzada en su tipo en operar antes de la puesta en marcha del macroproyecto internacional ITER en Francia. La meta del BEST es operar a pleno rendimiento experimental hacia finales de la década para lograr una ganancia neta de energía sostenible. A más largo plazo, los plazos fijados por la comunidad científica china apuntan a que los hallazgos en Hefei sirvan como base directa para la construcción del reactor de demostración comercial (CFETR). Este plan escalonado prevé conectar los primeros prototipos de plantas de fusión a la red eléctrica nacional hacia la década de 2030 o principios de 2040. De cumplirse el cronograma previsto, Hefei no solo habrá liderado el desarrollo científico del sector, sino que habrá situado a China en una posición de vanguardia en la generación de electricidad comercial mediante fusión nuclear.
